title: The Elastic Tournament: A Second Transformation of the Big Law Firm
author: Marc Galanter · William D. Henderson

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source supports ancillary parts of the cluster—especially client price pressure, profitability monitoring, staffing change and workload consequences—but it does not address whether AI-driven reductions in matter hours can preserve profits or how rates, costs and demand mediate that effect. It expressly leaves the economic stability of its own staffing model unresolved.
qs: Whether this model will be fundamentally “stable” in the economic sense remains to be seen.
Corporate clients are definitely interested in high-quality legal services at a predictable price.

st.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
st.an: The source provides historical context on large firms’ growing share of graduate recruitment and continued elite-school ambitions, but it predates and does not assess the current entry-level contraction, sector-specific slowdown or possible AI displacement. It therefore contextualises the cluster without taking a determinable position on its principal proposition.
qs: Over the last three decades, an increasing proportion of law school graduates are beginning their careers in large law firms.4 Based on the size of the 2007 summer associate classes, The American Lawyer magazine estimates that the nation’s two hundred largest law firms (based on revenue) are set to hire ten thousand entering associates during the fall of 2008.5 “That astonishing

To put it another way, the top 20 law schools will only produce about 6,500 graduates.”6 Because virtually all large law firms still aspire to some variant of the original “Cravath system,” in which the firm establishes its brand by hiring only the best students from the best law schools and providing them with the best       2.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source accepts that Big Law’s significance and survival cannot be assessed by size alone, then materially develops the cluster’s account by explaining how client sophistication, financial transparency and partner mobility transform the promotion tournament into career-long competition. Its evidence on non-equity tiers, de-equitization, retention incentives and market segmentation strengthens the cluster’s analysis of durable value alongside institutional fragility.
qs: Moreover, until a large law firm lawyer renounces any interest in prerogatives of ownership (e.g., a claim on residual profits, a voice in firm management), the duration of the tournament can now be expected to last one’s entire career.
1695, 1696 (1998) (arguing that the promotion-to- partnership tournament has become “only one factor among many that contribute to the organizational structure of the large law firm”).

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source accepts that stronger in-house departments shift purchasing control toward corporate buyers while outside firms remain important through task-specific engagements and elite, high-stakes matters. It materially extends the cluster by proposing a performance-led, non-hourly provider model for high-volume, price-sensitive corporate work.
qs: Further, a focus on job performance may be an ideal environment to develop the talents and abilities and women and minority attorneys, 265 who have not fared well in a tracked and seeded promotion-to-partnership tournament.266      Although general counsel may favor elite law firms for bet-the-company matters, this new business model could make substantial in-roads for higher volume, price-sensitive corporate work.

st.t: Cravath model: Modern firms retain hollowed labels
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s account of a hollowed-out Cravath model and materially develops it through the concept of an “elastic tournament”: permanent associates, non-equity partners and other non-tournament lawyers relax up-or-out and sever seniority from ownership. It also contributes evidence of widening firm stratification while appropriately treating the predicted recruitment-market split as prospective.
qs: • Abandoning the equation of seniority with ownership and acceptance           of permanent employee status for lawyers.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source accepts the tournament framework and materially extends it into an “elastic tournament” in which competition continues after partnership through differentiated compensation, non-equity tiers, de-equitization and forced exit. It also connects this career-long competition to reduced collective investment in training, ethics and firmwide capabilities, directly developing the cluster’s systems-level account.
qs: The diminution in sharing also reduces the time       horizons of individual lawyers and decreases their willingness to invest in       firmwide initiatives that do not simultaneously optimize their own practice.

st.t: Market reform: Information and incentives shape access
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s focus on information and incentives and materially develops it through evidence that sophisticated corporate buyers can impose stronger controls while competitive client-retention pressures weaken lawyers’ independent counseling. It also supports caution in interpreting reputational and disciplinary disparities across market segments.
qs: See GALANTER & PALAY, supra note 14, at 50 (“In their relationship with outside law firms, today’s enlarged corporate legal departments impose budgetary restraints, exert more control over cases, demand periodic reports, and engage in comparison shopping among firms.”); Mark C.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s claim that governance, ownership and mobility—not capital scarcity alone—shape law-firm adaptation. It supplies a pre-generative-AI account of how lateral mobility and portable clients weakened cohesion and produced a small owner core surrounded by permanent employee lawyers, while leaving the model’s stability unresolved.
qs: Clients and lawyers became more mobile, as long term retainer relationships with clients gave way and the lifetime commitment of lawyers to firms was threatened by the lateral movement of lawyers.

st.t: Professional independence: Regulation should follow client vulnerability
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster’s claim that professionalism depends on organizational conditions rather than any inherently superior practice setting. It combines Carlin’s evidence of greater ethical conformity in large firms with the qualification that ethical stressors—not size itself—explain the difference, and cites contrary evidence that corporate lawyers had less autonomy. It does not, however, recommend allocating regulatory authority by client vulnerability or harm.
qs: See, e.g., HEINZ & LAUMANN, supra note 44, at 365-73 (1982) (observing in a large-scale empirical study of Chicago lawyers during mid-1970s that corporate lawyers had less autonomy than their small firm counterparts).

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts the broader reconfiguration of legal-service production and materially extends it by identifying an earlier, non-AI institutional shift: large firms loosened up-or-out and incorporated permanent, contract, staff and outsourced lawyers. This supplies a staffing-side precursor to workflow unbundling, though it does not directly address buyer-led allocation, AI, verification or pricing reform.
qs: This transformation is the most drastic and significant metamorphosis in the large law firm since the invention and spread of the tournament firm in the closing years of the nineteenth century—a transformation that portends major shifts in the way that legal services are produced and delivered.

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central account: stronger in-house departments gain monitoring and purchasing power, while commercial dependence and corporate assimilation can weaken outside and in-house lawyers’ independent professional judgment. Its ethical effects are partly predictive, and it does not itself materially develop the cluster’s reciprocal-duty or contextual-regulation proposals.

kp.d: This historical study does not discuss AI. Galanter and Henderson argue that changes in corporate legal services transformed the traditional promotion-to-partnership tournament into an elastic competition encompassing associates and partners. Partnership increasingly ceases to guarantee ownership, financial security or eventual respite; lawyers compete throughout their careers unless they relinquish ownership aspirations.
qs: In short, the only finish line is death or retirement.

the fundamental economic reality that underlies this transformation is the inability of large law firms to underwrite a prize of partnership that includes both long-term financial security and eventual repose.

kp.k: An ownership core surrounds itself with employed lawyers
kp.d: The authors describe a core-and-mantle structure: owner-partners surrounded by associates, permanent associates, non-equity partners, of counsel and de-equitized former partners. Expanded employee categories relax up-or-out, disconnect seniority from ownership, and accommodate contract and outsourced lawyers. Their model concerns the upper corporate-law sector represented by the AmLaw 200 and NLJ 250, not all legal practice.
qs: a core of owner-partners is surrounded by a much larger mantle of employed lawyers
Nor do we claim that it holds throughout all tournament-based firms.
We do not know whether there is an analogous change within the personal services hemisphere.

kp.k: Aggregate partnership growth masks considerable firm-level instability
kp.d: The authors find a relatively smooth aggregate upward trajectory in NLJ 250 partnership ranks, while associate numbers track business cycles more closely. Among 236 firms appearing in both the 2006 and 2007 lists, partner counts increased by an average of ten per firm, but 58 firms (24.6%) reported decreases. They identify retirement, lateral defections and partnership pruning as possible explanations rather than isolating a single cause.
qs: the number of associates appears to coincide with the ebb and flow with the business cycle.
58 firms (24.6%) reported a diminution in the number of partners.

kp.k: Prestige produces different growth strategies and leverage ratios
kp.d: A comparison of 117 firms links partnership growth over 1978–2006 with FY 2005 profits per equity partner, distinguishing prestigious slow-growth firms, prestigious high-growth megafirms and medium-growth firms with lesser reputational endowments. The quadratic fit has R2 of 0.261 versus 0.133 for a linear fit. The ten slowest-growing firms averaged 2.59 associates per partner versus 1.39 for their faster-growing counterparts. The authors argue that reputation allows different strategies, while geographic coverage and client defense also drive growth independently of the tournament.
qs: they tend to have a much higher ratio of associates to partners (2.59 on average) than their faster growing counterparts (1.39 on average).
competition is a separate driver of growth for firms with lesser amounts of reputational capital.

kp.k: Non-equity tiers preserve promotion while restricting ownership
kp.d: Between 1993 and 2007, the proportion of NLJ 250 firms reporting at least one non-equity partner increased from 42.4% to 74.8%. In FY 2005, Am Law 200 equity partners increased only from 26,755 to 26,903, while non-equity partners rose from 10,780 to 12,235, a 13.5% increase. The authors interpret these tiers as a way to retain lawyers and sustain promotion incentives without diluting rainmakers' profits. They caution that firms withholding tier breakdowns may cause reported adoption to understate the change.
qs: the prize of equity partnership, which includes the traditional prerogatives of ownership, is increasingly rare.
the number of non-equity partners increased from 10,780 to 12,235—a 13.5% jump.

kp.k: Partner workloads rise as tenure protections weaken
kp.d: Drawing on Altman Weil longitudinal data for 1985–2003, the article reports average associate billable hours hovering around 1,850, while partners in their 25th to 29th year increased from 1538 to consistently above 1,700. The authors suggest fear of de-equitization as an explanation, rather than establishing causation. They also ask whether an increasingly unattractive partnership prize discourages associates from working additional hours.
qs: Perhaps the simplest explanation for these trends is the specter of de-equitization, which causes partners to work harder.
why bill more hours when the payoff of partnership is increasingly less attractive?

kp.k: Training and career prospects matter for associate retention
kp.d: A reported multivariate study of Am Law 200 midlevel associates associates intentions to remain at least two years with interesting work, higher-quality work, shorter weeks, family friendliness, a higher non-equity-to-equity partner ratio and clearer communication about partnership prospects. After controls, salary and bonus have no statistically significant relationship with intentions to stay. The outcome is stated retention intention, not observed subsequent attrition, and the authors interpret the importance of work quality partly through its contribution to future employability.
qs: After controlling for all of these factors, combined salary and bonus had no statistical relationship to midlevel associate’s desire to remain with the firm.
presumably because it enhances an associate’s human capital

kp.k: Technology and sophisticated buyers weaken enduring firm relationships
kp.d: The authors trace competition to stronger in-house departments, greater information availability, legal journalism, branch expansion and computing. Corporate counsel increasingly retain specialists for particular matters rather than rely on longstanding firm relationships. Internal financial systems and standardized electronic billing make lawyer, practice-group and firm performance more visible. They describe substantial, but explicitly incomplete, commoditization of corporate legal work.
qs: a substantial portion of corporate legal services—but not all—is in the process of being commoditized.
the economic contribution of specific lawyers or law firms has become more measurable and transparent.

kp.k: Lateral mobility privileges portable client relationships
kp.d: The ALM dataset contains 14,338 lawyer movements from January 2000 through December 2005, assembled primarily from destination firms' news releases. Annual movements rose from 1,998 to 2,752; 50.2% entered an Am Law 200 firm from outside that group, 28.3% moved within it, 18.4% left it for smaller firms and 3.1% moved among other settings into non-Am Law 200 firms. The authors report 96.8% of intra-Am Law 200 lateral movement occurring within the same regional market. They argue that firms restrict cross-subsidies to retain partners able to leave with clients.
qs: The sample, which was built primarily from news releases at each lawyer’s new firm, includes 14,338 lawyer movements from January 2000 through December 2005.
This structure reduces cross-subsidies between lawyers with differential value to the firm, thus reducing the potential for large-scale lateral defections.

kp.k: Practice specialties sort lawyers across differently profitable firms
kp.d: For 4,056 movements with financial data for both firms, mean firm PPP increased from $742,563 to $759,257, with substantial variation by specialty. An OLS model using 3,553 observations and adjusted R2 of 26.6% controls for prior firm PPP, fiscal year and major regional markets. Table 3 associates white-collar/securities enforcement, M&A/private equity/venture capital, antitrust and IP with higher destination-firm PPP; regulatory, labor and employment, real estate/public and project finance, and trusts and estates have negative coefficients. These are destination-firm profitability associations, not measurements of individual compensation. Although the prose says only bankruptcy lacks significance, Table 3 also reports corporate securities as non-significant at p = 0.139.
qs: For the sample as a whole, there is a movement toward more profitable firms (from $742,563 to $759,257).
both the magnitude of the gain (or loss) and the relative starting position of the firm left appear to be strongly influenced by practice setting.

kp.k: Salary competition may split elite and semi-elite firms
kp.d: The authors predict that profitable capital-markets practices will allow elite firms to escalate associate salaries beyond semi-elite competitors' reach. From the first Am Law 200 fiscal year in 1998 to the article's reported comparison, weighted average PPP rose 95.3%, from $926,571 to $1,809,935, in the most profitable quartile, versus 58.3%, from $287,909 to $455,780, in the bottom quartile. Contemporary responses include merit-based associate compensation, practice-specific pay and lower-paid off-track positions. Permanent market separation remains a prediction, not an established outcome.
qs: In the years to come, we predict that the law firms with a strong presence in the capital markets area will further raise the stakes in the salary wars and permanently separate themselves from their semi-elite counterpart.
the watering down of the Cravath system may open the door to new and innovative business and human capital strategies for lawyers.

kp.k: Mobility creates collective-action problems for firm governance
kp.d: The authors attribute weakened collective investment to structural incentives rather than simply greed: powerful partners can leave, making commitments to risk-sharing, training, diversity or reduced workloads difficult to sustain. Size and geographic dispersion weaken informal cultural restraints, while professional restrictions on non-compete agreements limit contractual retention. They acknowledge firms that continue to share risks and sustain collective loyalty. The abstract calls the model economically stable, but the conclusion explicitly leaves long-run stability unresolved.
qs: This outcome is dictated not by an absence of professional ideals but a widening and intractable collective action problem that undermines the requisite conditions for the embodiment of those ideals.
Whether this model will be fundamentally “stable” in the economic sense remains to be seen.

kp.k: Economic insecurity may undermine independent ethical judgment
kp.d: The authors use Jerome Carlin's early-1960s study of 800 New York private practitioners to argue that large firms' apparent ethical advantages reflected insulation from client and court pressures, not size alone. They contend that mobile clients, internal profitability pressures and de-equitization now erode that insulation. Qualitative studies are cited for the prominence of zealous advocacy. The article reports Ronald Gilson's proposal to relocate professional gatekeeping toward in-house lawyers, but also cites Nelson and Nielsen's evidence of commercial pressures within corporate departments. These support a structural argument about ethical vulnerability, not a quantified increase in misconduct.
qs: the ethical norm that is most widely embraced by large firm lawyers is the very one that reduces the strains in the lawyer-client relationship: zealous advocacy.
insecure lawyers will be less likely to acknowledge any black or white.

kp.k: Unequal developmental opportunities impede minority advancement
kp.d: Using After the JD findings, ABA studies and associate surveys, the article reports minority lawyers' poorer access to mentoring, client contact and developmental assignments. Its mechanism is an internal labor market where powerful partners allocate scarce training to associates expected to benefit their own practices. The authors discuss Richard Sander's contested grades-and-skills explanation but explicitly do not depend on it: stereotypes and perceived ability can produce unequal opportunities. Firm-wide recruitment benefits do not necessarily induce individual partners to bear development and retention costs.
qs: the actual outcome (or equilibrium) is primarily the result of an internal labor market in which partners and associates fend for themselves.
Our analysis, however, does not depend upon this interpretation.
the mere perception of lower ability based on stereotype is enough to reduce the flow of coveted work assignments and training opportunities.

kp.d: The article connects women's advancement barriers to unequal caregiving responsibilities and partners' demands for continuously available support. Indiana alumni data report childcare-related part-time work or non-employment for 1% of men versus 24% of women five years after graduation, and 2% versus 40% fifteen years after graduation. Michigan alumni evidence associates childcare-related time off with lower partnership attainment. The authors argue that formal flexibility policies cannot by themselves overcome decentralized work allocation: NALP reported 98% of law firm employers permitted part-time work, but only 5.4% of lawyers used it.
qs: female Michigan law graduates who had taken time off for children were also less likely to be law firm partners.
firm managers lack the leverage to impose a top-down policy for the benefit of female lawyers with children.

kp.k: Lifestyle reform faces partner incentives and applicant choices
kp.d: The article reports, rather than treats as proven, contemporary characterizations of Millennials as demanding flexibility, diversity and rewarding work. It examines Building a Better Legal Profession's rankings and proposals for reduced hours, proportional pay and continued partnership eligibility. The authors question whether managers can impose these arrangements on mobile partners, noting fixed overhead and staffing costs. They also argue that elite graduates' observed choices favor pay, prestige and future options despite less favorable working conditions, allowing elite firms to recruit without accepting the proposed reforms.
qs: Nonetheless, we cannot resist the urge to speculate.
Once again, there is no “firm” that can impose these lifestyle policies so long as it is made up of autonomous partners who can vote with their feet.
This is not necessarily a deal that the prestigious Wall Street firms need to accept.

kp.k: Process-based employment models offer a speculative alternative
kp.d: The authors foresee two possible responses, especially from semi-elite firms under salary pressure: broader recruitment from regional law schools and a corporate-style employer replacing the partnership tournament with advancement based on performance and matter management. The second model would emphasize firm-specific processes, predictable pricing, flat fees or other non-hourly arrangements, lower salaries and more manageable hours. They suggest it could serve price-sensitive corporate work and improve opportunities for women and minorities. Nonlawyer capital and profit-sharing could fund experimentation; the proposed model and benefits are possibilities rather than demonstrated results.
qs: it would be developing firm-specific capital by focusing on business processes that deliver high quality legal services at a cost-effective and predictable price.
Demonstrated management and teamwork skills resulting in successful client engagements would carry more weight than Ivy-league credentials.
Although general counsel may favor elite law firms for bet-the-company matters, this new business model could make substantial in-roads for higher volume, price-sensitive corporate work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The document makes no AI-specific claims. Galanter and Henderson instead describe a historical transformation of large law firms into an 'elastic tournament' and predict further differentiation in staffing and business models.
pts.d: The authors argue that competition for ownership now extends throughout lawyers' careers, with equity increasingly concentrated among partners controlling valuable client relationships and an expanding mantle of employed lawyers. They attribute this transformation to market and organisational changes, including information technology—not AI. They predict separation between elite and semi-elite firms and speculate that some firms could abandon the partnership tournament in favour of salaried employment, process-based service delivery and non-hourly pricing.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The historical account combines longitudinal law-firm data, lateral-movement analysis, prior empirical research and examples of changing employment policies; future business models are explicitly speculative.
pts.d: The authors examine NLJ 250 partnership growth and tier structures, Am Law financial data, and an ALM dataset of 14,338 lawyer movements during 2000–2005. Their regression analysis relates practice specialties to profitability at destination firms. They also draw on qualitative studies of large-firm lawyers, associate surveys, alumni research and reported changes in compensation and career tracks. These are evidence for their account of legal-market restructuring, not evidence of AI effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Published in 2008, the article describes changes over preceding decades and offers conditional, undated predictions for subsequent years.
pts.d: The authors expressly limit their observations to the upper reaches of corporate legal practice, particularly Am Law 200 and NLJ 250 firms, rather than all legal services. They describe a gradual, uneven transition. Their proposed employee-based business model is especially associated with semi-elite firms facing salary competition and associate attrition; outside investment is presented as a possible facilitator. The abstract calls the model economically stable, but the conclusion qualifies its long-term stability as unresolved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern large-firm owners and employees, corporate legal buyers, and lawyers whose advancement depends on training, mentoring and working-time arrangements.
pts.d: Rainmaking partners gain bargaining power while other partners face de-equitization and continuing performance pressure. Associates and other employed lawyers encounter more permanent off-track positions. The authors argue that individualised incentives weaken collective investment in mentoring, diversity and professional independence, particularly disadvantaging minority lawyers and women with family responsibilities. Their proposed process-based firms could offer more predictable prices for corporate clients and more manageable hours for employed lawyers, while elite firms retain high-stakes matters.
